notes.1a: Almost all candidates successfully completed the table of results and obtained results comparable with those expected. The temperature change in Experiment 4 should have been approximately double that of Experiment 1 and the temperature changes should have increased down the table. A small number of candidates recorded highly improbable initial temperatures that were under 10C. It was expected that all temperatures and temperature changes would be recorded to the same resolution, preferably the nearest half division on the thermometer – so to the nearest 0.5C.
notes.1b: Most candidates produced sensible graph scales; the most common being each large grid square being either 4 or 5C. Those who chose difficult scales often made errors in the plotting and so did not gain the credit available for the correct plotting of all five points. The best fit line could be either a curve or a straight line, depending on the data obtained in the experiments. Many candidates drew straight lines when the points were clearly on a curve of decreasing gradient, in these cases credit for the best fit line was not awarded.
notes.1c: Most candidates were able to continue their graph line to the right so that a reading could be made at 45cm3. A significant number of candidates did not include the unit (C) in their answer; all physical quantities should be accompanied by a unit.
notes.1d: The calculation of the energy given out was completed successfully by the majority of candidates.
notes.1e: Most candidates realised that the increased mass of anhydrous lithium chloride would result in an increased temperature change. However, to gain full credit, candidates were required to give a quantitative answer. Two different quantitative answer were accepted: • The temperature change would be double the temperature change of Experiment 1 because the mass of anhydrous lithium chloride had doubled. • The temperature change would be the same as Experiment 4 because the ratio of anhydrous lithium chloride : water was the same as in Experiment 4. Some candidates incorrectly based their explanation on more anhydrous lithium chloride requiring more energy to dissolve. As the process is exothermic, energy is released and not taken in.
notes.1f: The required answer was based on polystyrene acting as an insulator and so would reduce heat loss from the solution. Less heat energy lost would mean a larger temperature rise. A significant number of candidates based their answer on the polystyrene cup being a more accurate method of measuring a volume than a beaker.
notes.1g: (i) The vast majority of candidates correctly stated that a burette measures volumes more accurately than a measuring cylinder.
notes.1gii: This proved to be a demanding question. In the experiments, heat energy is given out and results in the temperature of the solution increasing. Heat energy lost from the system (the beaker) results in a smaller temperature increase. If the beaker is stood in a water-bath, then more heat energy will be transferred from the beaker to the water-bath and so the temperature change will be even smaller, or possibly so small so as to be not measurable with the apparatus provided. Water-baths maintain a constant temperature and so are not suitable when the dependent variable (the required outcome of the investigation) is the temperature change.
notes.2: Centres were provided with instructions for how to prepare solid J because iron(II) iodide is not readily available and use of ammonium iron(II) sulfate minimises the contamination of the sample with iron(III).
notes.2a: Most candidates correctly reported the formation of a green precipitate on the dropwise addition of aqueous sodium hydroxide. That precipitate should have remained when excess aqueous sodium hydroxide was added, although a number of candidates stated that the precipitate then dissolved; this is not possible.
notes.2b: The instructions tell candidates to add the sample of aqueous chlorine followed by the starch solution. The order of addition is important. It was clear that some candidates added the starch and then the chlorine. Addition of aqueous chlorine will result in the oxidation of iodide ions to iodine. This should have resulted in aqueous iodine, giving the solution a yellow, orange or brown colour. Addition of starch would then cause the formation of a blue-black precipitate. The observations were therefore a description of the colour changes. Candidates who did not follow the order of addition in the question would have missed the initial colour of the aqueous iodine formed.
notes.2c: This was the test for halide ions. As solid J contained iodide ions, a yellow precipitate was expected. Although some candidates stated that there was no change, most noted the formation of a precipitate. The identification of the colour of the precipitate is difficult but it is expected that candidates will be familiar with the qualitative test for halide ions and to be aware of the difficulty.
notes.2d: Most candidates correctly noted the formation of a precipitate. This precipitate should have been green or grey-green. Some candidates also noted the very small amount of effervescence that occurs as the carbonate ions react with the low concentration of hydrogen ions present in the solution.
notes.2e: Almost all candidates who had given correct observations then correctly identified solid J as iron(II) iodide. The oxidation state of the iron was required.
notes.2f: Candidates who performed well on Question 2 overall almost always reported the formation of a lilac flame. If the centre supervisor reported a different colour, then candidates were awarded credit for stating the same colour as the supervisor even if that colour was not lilac; this allows for a centre having a contaminated sample. Almost all supervisors reported the formation of a lilac flame.
notes.2g: (i) As the salt did not contain ammonium ions, there would not have been any ammonia formed and so the red litmus paper should not have changed. A common incorrect answer was to state that the red litmus paper became blue, this is either because that is what many candidates expect red litmus to do or because rather than holding the red litmus paper above the boiling tube they pushed it into the boiling tube and it touched the sides which had traces of aqueous sodium hydroxide on them.
notes.2gii: Candidates who performed well on Question 2 overall often correctly stated that either solid K was not an ammonium salt or that no ammonia had been made. A common incorrect answer was to say that an acid was made or that solid K was acidic; red litmus not changing does not show an acid has been made as red litmus can detect alkalis but not acids; blue litmus can detect acids but not alkalis.
notes.2iii: As the instructions say ‘Test any gas given off’ candidates were expected to report a positive test and result for a gas. As two marks were available, that means there must be another mark for an observation other than the positive gas test. The test conducted was the test for nitrate ions. Hence candidates were expected to test for ammonia gas using damp red litmus paper, which would have become blue. The expected other observation was that there was bubbling or fizzing of effervescence in the reaction mixture.
notes.2h: While many candidates correctly identified solid K as potassium nitrate, it was not uncommon for candidates to ignore their flame test result from 2(f).
notes.3: This planning task was a quantitative task and candidates were expected to make measurements as part of the plan. The most common appropriate methods seen involved: • using apparatus, such as a measuring cylinder, to put a stated volume of water in a suitable container such as a beaker or conical flask • warming the water to a temperature of 50C • describing some method of keeping the water at the required temperature, such as a water bath or insulated container • adding an excess of magnesium sulfate • stirring to speed up dissolving • filtering to remove the excess magnesium sulfate • then finding the mass of magnesium sulfate dissolved by either: • weighing the filtrate and subtracting from that the mass of the water used • drying the residue and subtracting the mass of the residue from original mass of the magnesium sulfate • evaporating the filtrate to dryness and finding the mass of the solid left. In all three cases, the mass found is the mass of magnesium sulfate dissolved in the volume of water used. Many excellent fully correct answers were seen. There were some common errors: • not identifying the apparatus used. Credit will not be given for a list of apparatus at the start of the plan, candidates need to state what the apparatus is used for • not stirring the mixture to help dissolve the magnesium sulfate. Relying just on diffusion means the experiment will take many hours • at the end, either not drying the residue from filtration or not evaporating to dryness the filtrate. Leaving the residue wet or just heating the filtrate to crystallising point will not give a correct answer • washing the residue obtained after filtration – this will cause more of it to dissolve and so any masses obtained will be incorrect • doing an extra step in the calculation of dividing the final answer by 100. If the volume of water used is 100 cm3 then the mass obtained is the solubility in g per 100 cm3 of water. One error that was seen a number of times was for candidates to measure the speed of dissolving rather than the mass that dissolved.
